questions.q: ShopFlow and the invoicing service want email receipts; the bookings app does not. Why build receipts as a plugin rather than as code inside ShopFlow?
questions.explain: A plugin is an optional feature behind a fixed interface. The host stays unchanged, and switching the feature on or off is a registration, not a code change. It still runs with the host's full power, so it can break the host.
options: Plugins run faster than application code
Each app decides with one register line whether it runs receipts, and the code exists once, outside every app
Plugins cannot have bugs that affect the host
Only plugins can listen to events

questions.q: The receipts plugin resolves the mailer from the container in initialize, not in install. Why?
questions.explain: install is where plugins offer things; initialize is where they can rely on everything that was offered. The mailer is a dependency, so its install would run first anyway, but initialize also works for services from plugins that are not dependencies.
options: install has no access to the container
The manager runs each phase for all plugins before the next, so by initialize every plugin, including the mailer, has finished install, where it registers its service
initialize runs before install
Resolving in install would throw a PluginStateError

questions.q: Why does the mailer call context.registerDisposable right after opening the connection in start, instead of closing the connection in its own dispose hook?
questions.explain: A dispose hook runs whenever the plugin is disposed, including after a failed or skipped start, and would have to guess what exists. Registering cleanup next to the acquisition makes rollback exact.
options: Because dispose hooks are never called
So the cleanup list only ever contains resources that really exist: a plugin that failed before opening, or was never started, has nothing to close
Because disposables run faster than hooks
Because dispose cannot be async

questions.q: Why is the plugin exported as createReceiptsPlugin() instead of a ready-made object?
questions.explain: A disposed plugin cannot be started again. Sharing one object between hosts or tests would also share its counters and subscriptions. A factory avoids both problems.
options: The manager only accepts functions
Each host and each test gets fresh state in its own closure, and a retry after a rollback needs new plugin objects anyway
Objects cannot have methods like health()
Factories make the plugin type-safe for register options

questions.q: The host grants allowedCapabilities: ["events"]. The receipts plugin declares ["events", "container"]. When does it fail?
questions.explain: The manager compares declared capabilities with the allow-list when the plugin is registered. It is a declaration check that catches mistakes, not a sandbox: a plugin can still do anything the process can.
options: At the first payment event
In the plugin's install hook
At manager.register, with a PluginRegistrationError naming the capability that is not granted
Never: capabilities are documentation only

questions.q: Receipts requires @mycompany/zudo-plugin-mailer@^2.0.0 and the host registers mailer 3.0.0. What has run when the error is thrown?
questions.explain: Resolution and version checks happen before the first phase, so there is nothing to roll back. The error is a PluginDependencyVersionError, a subclass of PluginDependencyError.
options: The mailer's install and start
Every install hook
No hook at all: dependencies and versions are checked at the beginning of manager.start
Only the receipts install hook

questions.q: A host writes manager.register(createReceiptsPlugin(), { form: "receipts@shopflow.ng" }), with form instead of from. The plugin is typed Plugin<Partial<ReceiptsOptions> | undefined>. What catches the typo?
questions.explain: In the published @zudojs/plugins, register(plugin, options?: unknown) accepts anything. Validating in install turns the typo into a failed start with a rollback, instead of receipts with no sender.
options: TypeScript, because register checks options against the plugin's type
The manager, because it compares options with the plugin's metadata
Only the plugin's own validation in install: register types its second argument as unknown
Nothing: the plugin runs without a sender

questions.q: Why does the receipts plugin check typeof context.container.resolve === "function" at run time?
questions.explain: The plugin context is deliberately minimal: plugins are expected to offer services. A plugin that consumes one depends on more than the type guarantees, so it checks and fails early with a message that says what the host must provide.
options: Because resolve is async
Because the context's PluginContainer type only promises register; a host may pass a container that cannot resolve, and the plugin wants a clear error in install instead of a crash later
Because tokens made with Symbol.for cannot be resolved
Because TypeScript forbids calling methods on the container

questions.q: Why is the mailer's container token Symbol.for("@mycompany/zudo-plugin-mailer:Mailer") rather than Symbol("Mailer") or createToken("Mailer")?
questions.explain: Symbol() and createToken() create a new, unique key per module evaluation. Symbol.for(key) is shared through the global registry, the same idea as the @zudojs/errors brand.
options: Containers only accept global symbols
Every copy of the contract module returns the same symbol, so receipts finds the service even if it loaded a different copy of the mailer package than the host
It makes the token shorter
Global symbols are private to the plugin

questions.q: Receipts lists the audit plugin under optionalDependencies. What does that do when audit is installed, and when it is not?
questions.explain: A present optional dependency takes part in ordering exactly like a required one; an absent one is ignored. Receipts never calls audit; audit listens for receipt.sent.
options: Installed: receipts calls audit directly. Not installed: start fails
Installed: audit starts before receipts, so it is listening before the first receipt. Not installed: nothing, receipts starts normally
Installed: audit starts after receipts. Not installed: a warning is logged
It has no effect on ordering; it is documentation

questions.q: When should one plugin talk to another through a declared dependency and a container service, and when through events?
questions.explain: A dependency makes the manager guarantee presence and order. An event keeps the announcer unaware of its listeners, so audit, statistics or anything else can be added without touching receipts.
options: Always events: dependencies create coupling
Always dependencies: events are unreliable
A dependency and a service when you need something done and its result (receipts needs the mailer to send); events when you announce what happened and do not care who listens (receipt.sent for audit)
Dependencies for sync code, events for async code

questions.q: The payment.succeeded handler starts sendReceipt and tracks it in inFlight, but does not await it. Why?
questions.explain: The payment already succeeded; the receipt is follow-up work. Awaiting it would make every checkout as slow as the mail server. Tracking the promise lets stop wait for it at shutdown.
options: Because event handlers cannot be async
So the host's publishEvent, part of the payment request, returns at once instead of waiting for the mail server
Because awaiting would send the receipt twice
Because inFlight only accepts unresolved promises

questions.q: What is the difference between the receipts plugin's stop and its disposal?
questions.explain: Finishing work needs the resources still in place, so it comes first. Releasing comes after, newest first, and also runs for plugins that never started.
options: None; they are two names for one step
stop finishes work (refuses new payments, waits for receipts in flight); disposal then releases resources (unsubscribes, clears timers) through the disposables list
stop releases resources; disposal logs a summary
Disposal only runs if stop threw

questions.q: When does a plugin's context.signal abort?
questions.explain: The manager aborts each plugin's own signal at the start of its disposal. That is why the mailer's send takes the signal: a receipt that outlived stop fails fast instead of writing to a closed connection.
options: When its start hook returns
As soon as manager.stop is called, before any stop hook
When the plugin is disposed, just before its disposables run, so work still in progress sees the shutdown before resources disappear under it
Never: the host must abort it

questions.q: manager.diagnostics() reports the receipts plugin healthy, yet its last three receipts bounced. Why, and what fixes it?
questions.explain: Only the plugin knows whether its work succeeds. A health endpoint that combines lifecycle state with each plugin's own report catches a running-but-failing plugin.
options: The diagnostics are cached; call them again
Diagnostics derive health from the lifecycle state only (started means healthy); the plugin offers its own health() and the host reports both
Bounces are not errors
The manager only checks health during start

questions.q: Mailer and receipts are started; then SMS alerts, which depends on receipts, throws in start. In what order are things undone?
questions.explain: Rollback stops what was started in reverse dependency order, then disposes everything that holds resources in the same reverse order, including the failed plugin. The mailer's connection closes last because others depended on it.
options: Mailer stopped, receipts stopped, then disposed in registration order
Receipts stopped, mailer stopped; then SMS alerts, receipts and mailer disposed, dependents first
Only SMS alerts is disposed; the others keep running
Everything is disposed at once, in parallel

questions.q: In the published @zudojs/plugins, what does catch (error) around manager.start receive when a plugin's start throws new Error("key rejected")?
questions.explain: PluginStartError is exported but the manager never throws it. The lesson's startPlugins helper finds the failed plugin in the diagnostics and wraps the error, keeping the original as cause.
options: A PluginStartError whose pluginName names the plugin
The plugin's own Error("key rejected"), unwrapped; the plugin's name is only in diagnostics()
An AggregateError of all failures
Nothing: start resolves and logs the error

questions.q: After a rolled-back start, you fix the configuration and call manager.start(context) again on the same manager. What happens?
questions.explain: Disposal is final by design, so a released resource can never be used again. Factories make "new plugin objects" a one-line change.
options: The plugins start normally
Only the failed plugin is retried
It throws PluginStateError: the plugins are disposed, and the state machine has no way back. Create a new manager with new plugin objects
It waits until the old start finishes
It starts the plugins twice

questions.q: With hookTimeout: 200, a plugin's start returns a promise that never settles. The host starts plugins before its HTTP server listens. What happens under plain Node?
questions.explain: An unref'd timer does not keep Node running. With no socket, timer or other work pending, Node ends the process. Holding the process open during start-up (the lesson's keepAlive interval) lets the timeout fire.
options: PluginTimeoutError after 200 ms, then rollback
The process waits forever
Node exits with code 13 ("unsettled top-level await") without a timeout error or rollback, because the manager's timeout timer is unref'd and nothing else keeps the process alive
The manager retries the hook

questions.q: Version 1.3.0 of your plugin adds "network" to its capabilities. Why is that a breaking change?
questions.explain: Capabilities are part of the contract with the host. Requiring a new one is like requiring a new peer dependency: installations that worked yesterday stop working, so it belongs in a major version.
options: It changes the plugin's name
Every host whose allowedCapabilities does not include "network" now fails at register after upgrading
Capabilities are only read at build time
It is not breaking; capabilities are optional

questions.q: The receipts package lists @mycompany/zudo-plugin-mailer in peerDependencies and the receipts plugin lists it in dependencies. What does each one check?
questions.explain: A host could have the package installed but register a different mailer plugin, or none. The two ranges should agree, and each guards a different mistake.
options: They check the same thing twice
The peer dependency makes npm install a compatible mailer package on disk; the plugin dependency makes the manager check the mailer plugin the host actually registered
The peer dependency checks at run time, the plugin dependency at install time
Only the plugin dependency matters; npm ignores peers

questions.q: The host moves payment.succeeded from the in-process bus to a message queue that delivers at least once. What must the receipts plugin add?
questions.explain: "At least once" means duplicates will happen. Deduplicating by a stable key makes the handler idempotent, exactly like the payment service's reference check.
options: Nothing: the plugin cannot tell the difference
A longer hookTimeout
A record of sent receipts by payment reference, so a duplicate delivery does not email the customer twice
An optional dependency on the queue plugin

questions.q: The host passes an @zudojs/events bus in the plugin context. The manager publishes plugin:started. Which subscription receives every plugin lifecycle event?
questions.explain: plugin:started becomes plugin.started when published. A namespace wildcard matches it; plugin:* is not a valid pattern, because a wildcard is only allowed as the last segment after a dot.
options: events.on("plugin:*", …)
events.on("plugin.*", …), because the bus normalizes : to . and plugin.* matches every plugin. type
events.on("*plugin*", …)
None: lifecycle events are internal to the manager

questions.q: Write startOrder(plugins): every plugin after all its deps, and after its optional dependencies that are present in plugins; missing optional ones are ignored. Visit plugins in the given order. The program should print db mailer audit receipts api.
questions.explain: A depth-first visit adds a plugin only after its dependencies. api needs receipts, which needs mailer (which needs db) and the present optional audit; sms is not registered, so it is skipped. Any order that respects every dependency would be valid; this one follows the declaration order of each plugin's dependencies, as the manager does.

questions.q: Write createScope() returning onDispose(fn) and async disposeAll(): run the handlers newest first, keep going when one throws, and at the end throw an AggregateError with all failures (if any). The program should print timer cleared, connection closed, 1 failure: unsubscribe failed.
questions.explain: One failing cleanup must not strand the others: the connection still closes. Collecting every failure, as the manager's PluginDisposeError does in its errors, keeps the report complete.

timer cleared
connection closed
1 failure: unsubscribe failed

questions.q: Write startPlugins(start, diagnostics): call start(); if it throws, find the failed plugin in diagnostics() and throw a PluginStartError from @zudojs/errors with the message Plugin "NAME" failed to start: MESSAGE, the plugin name, and the original error as cause. The program should print the two lines in expected.
questions.explain: The manager's diagnostics know which plugin failed; its thrown error does not. Combining the two gives operators a message that names the plugin, and code a typed error with the original cause.
questions.expected:
Plugin "sms-alerts" failed to start: SMS gateway rejected the API key
true sms-alerts SMS gateway rejected the API key

questions.q: Write parseOptions(value) for a statistics plugin: intervalMs must be an integer of at least 1000, and label a non-empty string. Report all problems in one TypeError joined by "; ", else return the options. The program should print ok 60000 sales, then intervalMs must be an integer >= 1000; label must be a non-empty string.
questions.explain: Called from install, a validator like this turns bad settings into a failed start with a rollback and a message that lists every problem at once.
questions.expected:
ok 60000 sales
intervalMs must be an integer >= 1000; label must be a non-empty string

questions.q: Write createTracker(limit) with success(), failure() and status(): status() returns "degraded" once there have been limit failures in a row, and "healthy" otherwise; a success resets the count. The program should print healthy healthy degraded healthy.
questions.explain: Counting failures in a row separates "one mailbox bounced" from "the mail system is down", and the reset on success lets health recover without a restart.

questions.q: Complete stop(): stop accepting new jobs, wait for every job in flight (successful or failed) and return how many were waiting. The program should print drained 3, done: 2 ok, 1 failed, after stop: rejected.
questions.explain: Refuse new work first, or the drain may never end. allSettled waits for failures too, so one bounced mail cannot cut the drain short. In the plugin, hookTimeout puts an upper limit on this wait.
questions.expected:
drained 3
done: 2 ok, 1 failed
after stop: rejected

questions.q: The plugin system adapts an event bus (publishEvent({ type, payload }) and on(type, handler) returning a subscription) to the simpler on/off/emit interface plugins use, where handlers receive only the payload. Write toPluginEvents(bus). The program should print receipt for ORD-7 once: after off, the second publish reaches nobody.
questions.explain: off receives the plugin's handler, but the bus knows only the wrapper it was given, so the adapter must remember which subscription belongs to which handler. The real toPluginEvents keys that map by event name and handler.

questions.q: Write register(plugin, allowed) that throws an Error with the message Plugin "NAME" requests capabilities that are not granted: A, B. when the plugin's metadata.capabilities include anything outside allowed, and otherwise returns "registered NAME". The program should print the two lines in expected.
questions.explain: Listing every denied capability, not just the first, lets the operator decide in one step whether to grant them or drop the plugin. The check runs at registration, before the plugin's code has done anything.
questions.expected:
registered receipts
Plugin "exporter" requests capabilities that are not granted: network, filesystem.
